claim: March Mammal Madness reaches hundreds of thousands of people in the United States every year.
source: March Mammal Madness is a science outreach project that, over the course of several weeks in March, reaches hundreds of thousands of people in the United States every year.
evidence: The abstract states this directly, and later sections provide specific numbers (e.g., ~245,000 students in 2019).

claim: March Mammal Madness combines four approaches to science outreach: gamification, social media platforms, community event(s), and creative products.
source: We combine four approaches to science outreach – gamification, social media platforms, community event(s), and creative products – to run a simulated tournament in which 64 animals compete to become the tournament champion.
evidence: The abstract explicitly lists these four approaches as components of the MMM design.

claim: The outcomes of March Mammal Madness battles rely on empirical evidence from the scientific literature.
source: While the encounters between the animals are hypothetical, the outcomes rely on empirical evidence from the scientific literature.
evidence: The abstract states this directly, and the manuscript provides data on citations used (N=1078 scholarly sources).

claim: To date, approximately 1100 scholarly works covering almost 400 taxa have been transformed into science stories through March Mammal Madness.
source: To date ~1100 scholarly works, covering almost 400 taxa, have been transformed into science stories.
evidence: The abstract provides these specific numbers, which are supported by data in Figure 6 and the text (N=1078 scholarly sources, N=383 species).

claim: March Mammal Madness is most typically used by high-school educators teaching life sciences.
source: March Mammal Madness is most typically used by high-school educators teaching life sciences, and we estimate that our materials reached ~1% of high-school students in the United States in 2019.
evidence: The abstract states this, and survey data show that N=1099 of N=1589 educators taught high school grades 9-12.

claim: March Mammal Madness materials reached approximately 1% of high-school students in the United States in 2019.
source: March Mammal Madness is most typically used by high-school educators teaching life sciences, and we estimate that our materials reached ~1% of high-school students in the United States in 2019.
evidence: The abstract provides this estimate, which is supported by the survey data showing N=245,483 students in 2019.

claim: Human psychological and cognitive adaptations for shared experiences, social learning, narrative, and imagery contribute to the widespread use of March Mammal Madness.
source: Here we document the intentional design, public engagement, and magnitude of reach of the project. We further explain how human psychological and cognitive adaptations for shared experiences, social learning, narrative, and imagery contribute to the widespread use of March Mammal Madness.
evidence: The abstract states this as a goal of the manuscript, and the discussion section provides citations and reasoning about these adaptations.

claim: A substantial portion of empirical research and research infrastructure in higher education is supported through public funds.
source: A substantial portion of empirical research and research infrastructure, especially in higher education, is supported through public funds.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to Hazelkorn and Gibson, 2019.

claim: Research output is expected to serve the public good.
source: Research output is therefore not only expected to serve the public good (Hazelkorn and Gibson, 2019), but a broad view of the social contract conceptually situates scientific knowledge generated with public funds within the public trust (Schroeder et al., 1989; Gibbons, 1999; Hetland, 2017; Krishna, 2020; for important exceptions, see Fox, 2020).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Even when scholarly publications are open access, empirical findings too often remain behind a paywall of jargon.
source: Advocacy for Open Science has grown in recent decades (Sá and Grieco, 2016; Cribb and Sari, 2010; Piwowar et al., 2018; NASEM, 2018) but even when scholarly publications are open access, empirical findings too often remain behind a paywall of jargon.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the introduction as a motivation for science communication efforts.

claim: Institutions, funding agencies, professional societies, and individual scholars increasingly recognize the importance of science communication and informal STEM education.
source: As such, institutions, funding agencies, professional societies, and individual scholars increasingly recognize the importance of science communication (hereafter SciComm) and informal STEM education to reach learners, clinicians, policy-makers, and other members of the general public (Beaulieu et al., 2018; Jessani et al., 2018; Bell, 2016; National Science Board, 2011; Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Increased visibility of science and scientists can counter stereotypes about who does science and inspire the next generation of scientists.
source: Moreover, increased visibility of science and scientists can counter stereotypes about who does science and inspire the next generation of scientists (Woods-Townsend et al., 2016; Jarreau et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations.

claim: Scholars across the life, biomedical, physical, and social sciences participate in science communication and educational outreach.
source: Across the life, biomedical, physical, and social sciences, scholars participate in SciComm and educational outreach (Yuan et al., 2019; Cooke et al., 2017), and increasingly leverage social media platforms to achieve these broader impacts (Bik et al., 2015; Collins et al., 2016; McClain and Neeley, 2014; Mehlenbacher, 2019; Jarreau et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Science communication and educational outreach campaigns can be variably successful in their content, reach, propagation, and sustainability.
source: SciComm and educational outreach campaigns, however, can be variably successful in their content, reach, propagation, and sustainability and "impact" is often opaquely operationalized, measured, or assessed (Saunders et al., 2017; Davies, 2019).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations.

claim: Web traffic, social media engagement, and long-term use of resources are most often used as indicators of science communication impact.
source: Web traffic, social media engagement, and long-term use of resources are most often used as indicators of SciComm impact (Saunders et al., 2017; Fernández-Bellon and Kane, 2020).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations.

claim: Memes, images, activities, and dynamic content from scientists are associated with increased learner and public interest, competencies, donations, and enthusiasm for nature.
source: Early and recent reports, however, have demonstrated that memes, images, activities, and dynamic content from scientists are associated with increased learner and public interest, competencies, donations, and enthusiasm for nature (Moskal et al., 2007; Hone et al., 2011; McClure et al., 2020; McClain, 2019; Lenda et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Students in the United States are particularly interested in animal behavior.
source: Science communicators have previously recognized that students in the United States are particularly interested in animal behavior (Bush et al., 2018) across urban, suburban, and rural landscapes in which species diversity and visibility varies (Schuttler et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations.

claim: At very young ages, children are attracted to neotenous and familiar animal phenotypes.
source: At very young ages, children are attracted to neotenous and familiar animal phenotypes (Borgi et al., 2014; Borgi and Cirulli, 2015).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations.

claim: Children and young adults express greater affinity for mammals and birds than reptiles, insects, and amphibians.
source: Children and young adults also express greater affinity for mammals and birds than reptiles, insects, and amphibians (Schlegel and Rupf, 2010).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation.

claim: March Mammal Madness makes accessible reports from the scientific literature including elegant behavioral ecology experiments, meticulous natural history descriptions, and gripping narratively-constructed accounts of observed animal behavior.
source: Leveraging the dynamic game elements of a single elimination tournament combined with story-telling scientists, March Mammal Madness makes accessible reports from the scientific literature including elegant behavioral ecology experiments (Morand-Ferron et al., 2016; Campbell et al., 2009), meticulous natural history descriptions (Able, 2016; Tewksbury et al., 2014), and gripping narratively-constructed accounts of observed animal behavior (Ramsay and Teichroeb, 2019).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations to specific types of literature.

claim: The tournament provides lesson plans as an Open Educational Resource to educators.
source: The tournament also provides lesson plans as an Open Educational Resource (Miao et al., 2016) to educators who systematically integrate March Mammal Madness into their curriculum.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation defining Open Educational Resources.

claim: March Mammal Madness achieves key science communication goals by reaching many audiences, facilitating interactions between scientists and students, and effecting propagation and sustained adoption of the tournament.
source: March Mammal Madness achieves key SciComm goals by reaching many audiences (Varner, 2014), facilitating interactions between scientists and students (Boyette and Ramsey, 2019), and effecting propagation and sustained adoption of the tournament (Stanford et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations to relevant SciComm literature.

claim: Each March, dozens of academics, conservationists, and artists use Twitter to deliver performance science in the form of a simulated tournament.
source: Each March, dozens of academics, conservationists, and artists use the social media stage of Twitter to deliver performance science in the form of a simulated tournament to reveal an annual animal champion (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Each year, March Mammal Madness releases a unique bracket revealing the selected combatants organized into four thematic divisions.
source: Each year, we release a unique bracket revealing the selected combatants organized into four thematic divisions.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by Table 1 showing divisions across years.

claim: Players predict the likely outcomes of sequential encounters between pairs of combatants based on the player's knowledge, preferences, or taxon allegiances.
source: Players predict the likely outcomes of sequential encounters between pairs of combatants based on the player's knowledge, preferences, or taxon allegiances.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated in the description of how the tournament works.

claim: Scientist-narrators 'live-announce' the crafted encounters like a sporting event radiocast on Twitter.
source: Scientist-narrators "live-announce" the crafted encounters like a sporting event radiocast on the social media platform Twitter, as players follow along, primarily via mobile devices (53%) or desktop/laptop computers (41%).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and includes data on device usage.

claim: Players follow along primarily via mobile devices (53%) or desktop/laptop computers (41%).
source: Scientist-narrators "live-announce" the crafted encounters like a sporting event radiocast on the social media platform Twitter, as players follow along, primarily via mobile devices (53%) or desktop/laptop computers (41%).
evidence: This claim provides specific percentages for device usage.

claim: Scientist-narrators typically use a standardized narrative arc, presenting background 'stats' for each combatant, describing the scene of the 'battle,' and then creatively reporting the back-and-forth details of the encounter like a sports play-by-play.
source: Scientist-narrators typically use a standardized narrative arc, in sequence presenting background "stats" for each combatant, describing the scene of the "battle," and then creatively report the back-and-forth details of the encounter like a sports play-by-play (see Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and references supplementary files with examples.

claim: March Mammal Madness is systematically anchored to the scientific literature.
source: Although rife with pop culture jokes and internet memes, March Mammal Madness is systematically anchored to the scientific literature (Hinde et al., 2017; Fisher, 2018).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations and data on scholarly sources used.

claim: For each simulated battle, scientist-narrators provide key information about each combatant species including facts about behavior, life history, conservation status, phylogeny, morphology, and other exceptional adaptations.
source: For each simulated battle, scientist-narrators provide key information about each combatant species and feature facts about behavior, life history, conservation status, phylogeny, morphology, and other exceptional adaptations.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated in the description of battle narrations.

claim: March Mammal Madness has featured 383 species from 2013-2019.
source: March Mammal Madness has featured hundreds of species from a global distribution of biogeographic regions (N = 383 species across 2013–2019).
evidence: This specific number is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2.

claim: Combatants have represented 25 out of 27 mammalian orders, all except Paucituberculata and Microbiotheria.
source: Combatants have represented N = 25/27 mammalian orders, all except for Paucituberculata and Microbiotheria.
evidence: This claim provides specific numbers and names the excluded orders.

claim: Carnivora, Artiodactyla, and Diprotodontia are particularly over-represented as tournament combatants.
source: Carnivora, Artiodactyla, and Diprotodontia are particularly over-represented as tournament combatants (Figure 2) and taxa from these orders have more often been featured in two or more tournament years as repeat entrants.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Chiroptera, Rodentia, and Eulipotyphla have been under-represented in proportion to their actual species counts.
source: Chiroptera, Rodentia, and Eulipotyphla are consistently featured as combatants, but have been under-represented in proportion to their actual species counts, while small-bodied taxa from mammalian orders less familiar to the general public have been routinely showcased (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: 53 non-mammal combatants have been included in March Mammal Madness from 2013 to 2019.
source: Although the tournament particularly celebrates Class Mammalia, many non-mammal combatants have been included in March Mammal Madness; N = 53 in total from 2013 to 2019.
evidence: This specific number is stated in the text.

claim: Since 2018, March Mammal Madness has featured dozens of diverse animal taxa including insect, amphibian, lepidosaurian, archosaurian (including avian), cephalopod, arachnid, crustacean, and tardigrade combatants.
source: While early tournaments only showcased a smattering of non-mammals, since 2018 March Mammal Madness has featured dozens of diverse animal taxa including insect, amphibian, lepidosaurian, archosaurian (including avian), cephalopod, arachnid, crustacean, and tardigrade combatants.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated with specific taxonomic groups listed.

claim: Several plant species were included in March Mammal Madness in 2019.
source: In an effort to further expand the topics included in our science outreach and to intentionally disrupt "plant blindness" (Jose et al., 2019), we included several plant species in 2019.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and includes a citation about plant blindness.

claim: Organismal diversity and description have waned as foci within biology curricula, in tandem with decreases in student and public engagement with nature.
source: Organismal diversity and description have waned as foci within biology curricula, in tandem with decreases in student and public engagement with nature (Tewksbury et al., 2014; Greene, 2005; Schmidly, 2005).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Early rounds of the tournament favor the better-ranked combatant by situating the encounter in their own habitat, a 'home-court advantage'.
source: Early rounds of the tournament favor the better-ranked combatant by situating the encounter in their own habitat, a "home-court advantage" that potentially disadvantages their opponent.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated in the description of battle locations.

claim: Adaptations mismatched with ecological context have contributed to tournament losses due to hyperthermia, hypoxia, and osmotic imbalance.
source: Adaptations mismatched with ecological context have contributed to tournament losses due to hyperthermia (Panthera uncia, Gulo gulo), hypoxia (Mustela erminea), and osmotic imbalance (Octopus vulgaris).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated with specific examples of species and physiological challenges.

claim: More advanced rounds are randomized among four possible ecosystems specific to each tournament year.
source: More advanced rounds – the Elite Trait, the Final Roar, and the Championship – are randomized among four possible ecosystems specific to each tournament year (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: Scientist-narrators often situate battles in specific locations to highlight national parks, conservation areas, public lands and/or endangered ecosystems.
source: Scientist-narrators often situate battles in specific locations to highlight national parks, conservation areas, public lands and/or endangered ecosystems (Bland et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation.

claim: Impacts of the human-driven global climate crisis, such as extreme sea ice retreat, permafrost thaw-slumping, and range constriction on altitudinal gradients have been decisive factors in battle outcomes.
source: Impacts of the human-driven global climate crisis, such as extreme sea ice retreat (Durner et al., 2011), permafrost thaw-slumping (Wang et al., 2014), and range constriction on altitudinal gradients (Henry et al., 2012) have been decisive factors in battle outcomes.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations to specific climate impacts.

claim: Technical knock out (TKO) outcomes occurred in approximately 50% of tournament battles (N=225/451).
source: TKO outcomes occurred in ~50% of tournament battles (N=225/451).
evidence: This claim provides specific data on battle outcome frequencies.

claim: Withdrawals from encounters occurred in 32% of battles (N=146/451).
source: But in nature the injury risks and/or energy costs associated with physical attacks, when weighed against potential benefit, can frequently precipitate de-escalation, retreat, or withdrawal (Parker and Rubenstein, 1981; Archer et al., 1994; Briffa and Sneddon, 2007), outcomes often intentionally featured in March Mammal Madness (32%, N=146/451).
evidence: This claim provides specific data on withdrawal outcomes and cites literature on animal behavior.

claim: Deus ex Machina outcomes occurred in 5.5% of battles (N=25/451).
source: The device of Deus ex Machina, resolution via an unexpected and external agent, is used by scientist-narrators to highlight important sources of mortality for species, account for improbable outcomes forced by improbable outcome randomization, or to diversify story arcs across battles. While only a small proportion of outcomes (5.5%, N=25/451), the Deus ex Machina device often incenses players, but suggests particularly strong long-term retention of information.
evidence: This claim provides specific data on Deus ex Machina outcomes.

claim: 'Other' outcomes occurred in 12% of battles (N=55/451).
source: "Other" outcomes (12%, N=55/451) featured in March Mammal Madness battles include prioritization of foraging, dam-building, nest relocation, distraction by mating competition, electrocution (Kumar and Kumar, 2015), Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (Blumstein et al., 2015), foraging exclusion, displacement, and cryptic hiding.
evidence: This claim provides specific data on 'other' outcomes and cites examples.

claim: On average, 22% of battle outcomes involved an 'upset' in which the worse-seeded species advanced.
source: Typically, the better-seeded species defeated the worse-seeded species, but on average 22% (mean=13 ± 2.2 sd) of battle outcomes involved an "upset" in which the worse-seeded species advanced.
evidence: This claim provides specific statistical data on upset frequencies.

claim: In the NCAA men's basketball March Madness tournament, historically approximately 22% of outcomes have been characterized as 'upsets'.
source: In the NCAA men's basketball March Madness tournament, historically ~22% of outcomes have been characterized as "upsets" (Greenburg, 2019).
evidence: This claim provides a comparison statistic and cites a source.

claim: Events occurring in one round are carried forward in a combatant's story arc.
source: Events occurring in one round are carried forward in a combatant's story arc. Combatants advancing in the tournament have had to grapple with snapped canines, wrenched knee joints, wound infections, envenomations, and zoonotic disease transmissions.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated with examples of carried-forward consequences.

claim: Tournament champions are most typically apex predators or large-bodied herbivores.
source: Tournament champions are most typically apex predators or large-bodied herbivores – African elephant (Loxodonta africana, 2013), spotted hyena clan (Crocuta crocuta, 2014), Sumatran rhinoceros (Dicerorhinus sumatrensis, 2015), tundra wolf (Canis lupus occidentalis, 2016), middle Pleistocene short-faced running bear (Arctodus simus, 2017), pygmy hippo (Choeropsis liberiensis, 2018), and Bengal tiger (Panthera tigris tigris, 2019).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and lists all champions from 2013-2019.

claim: To date, a non-mammal has yet to achieve tournament champion.
source: To date, a non-mammal has yet to achieve tournament champion, a state of affairs entirely due to empirically-grounded probabilities within the tournament structure and certainly not due to taxonomic biases (Batt, 2009; Schlegel and Rupf, 2010) that influence research effort and the scholarly literature (Jarić et al., 2019; Bezanson and McNamara, 2019) or the tournament architect.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated with a humorous acknowledgment of potential bias.

claim: Eleven artists have created 669 depictions of combatant species for the March Mammal Madness tournament.
source: Eleven artists have created N = 669 depictions of combatant species for the March Mammal Madness tournament.
evidence: This claim provides specific numbers for artists and artworks.

claim: Charon Henning joined March Mammal Madness leadership as tournament art director in 2015.
source: After playing the tournament in 2014, tattoo artist and scientific illustrator Charon Henning approached the narrators and offered to contribute artwork of the combatants. In 2015, Henning joined MMM leadership as tournament art director.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Artists have used both digital approaches and traditional illustration media, including graphite, pen and ink, scratchboard, and acrylic paints.
source: Artists have used both digital approaches and traditional illustration media, including graphite, pen and ink, scratchboard, and acrylic paints, to depict each of the competitors (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: By the completion of the tournament, the champion competitor has been depicted in seven individual illustrations.
source: First round artwork has generally been produced with a minimum of detail, while illustrations for advances became sequentially more refined. As a result, by the completion of the tournament, the champion competitor has been depicted in seven individual illustrations.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated based on the tournament structure.

claim: Beginning in 2016, the championship portrait has been an art fusion with contributions from each illustrator involved in that year's tournament.
source: Beginning in 2016, the championship portrait has been an art fusion with contributions from each illustrator involved in that year's tournament.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated about the collaborative championship artwork.

claim: All revenue generated by the sale of tournament artwork through the Society6 shop is equitably divided among the artistic team.
source: All revenue generated by the sale of tournament artwork through the Society6 shop (https://society6.com/mammalmadness) is equitably divided among the artistic team.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated about revenue sharing.

claim: March Mammal Madness battles from 2013 until the 2019 Championship included citations to 1078 scholarly sources.
source: Since the tournament's inception in 2013 until the 2019 Championship, March Mammal Madness battles included citations to N = 1078 scholarly sources, including N = 1016 peer-reviewed journal articles from N = 350 journals.
evidence: This claim provides specific numbers for citations used.

claim: March Mammal Madness battles included 1016 peer-reviewed journal articles from 350 journals.
source: Since the tournament's inception in 2013 until the 2019 Championship, March Mammal Madness battles included citations to N = 1078 scholarly sources, including N = 1016 peer-reviewed journal articles from N = 350 journals.
evidence: This claim provides specific numbers for peer-reviewed articles and journals.

claim: The number of scholarly publications cited each year has generally increased across the tournament years.
source: The number of scholarly publications cited each year has generally increased across the tournament years (Figure 6A), showing marked increases in conjunction with expansions of the narration team in 2014 (N = 4 scientist-narrators) and 2017 (N = 11 scientist-narrators).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: The Journal of Mammalogy, PLoS One, and the Journal of Zoology are most frequently cited by scientist-narrators.
source: The Journal of Mammalogy, PLoS One, and the Journal of Zoology are most frequently cited by scientist-narrators, and many other animal-focused and general science journals are represented among the top-cited journals in March Mammal Madness (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6B.

claim: The majority of scholarly sources (64%, N=689) were published in the 21st century.
source: The majority of scholarly sources, N = 689 (64%), were published in the 21 st century (Figure 6C), but some citations included writings dating back to the 1700s including important germinal studies of animal behavior and natural history (Burghardt, 2020).
evidence: This claim provides specific data on publication dates and is illustrated in Figure 6C.

claim: Experimental and explanatory science has increasingly displaced descriptive natural history, a significant loss to science and society that has been decried for decades.
source: Naturalists' detailed, integrative descriptions of behavioral and physical characteristics are excellent for crafting MMM narratives, although experimental and explanatory science has increasingly displaced descriptive natural history, a significant loss to science and society that has been decried for decades (Tewksbury et al., 2014; Greene, 2005; Schmidly, 2005).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Beginning in 2015, the American Society of Mammalogists has systematically featured 241 unique photographs of combatant taxa from the ASM Mammal Images Library.
source: Beginning in 2015, the American Society of Mammalogists (ASM), via the Informatics Committee, has systematically featured 241 unique photographs of combatant taxa from the ASM Mammal Images Library.
evidence: This claim provides specific numbers and dates for ASM contributions.

claim: The ASM Mammal Images Library is a curated collection of over 4700 high-resolution images of extant and extinct mammalian species.
source: As a nonprofit, educational program of the society, the Mammal Images Library is a curated collection of >4700 high-resolution images of extant and extinct mammalian species.
evidence: This claim provides specific information about the ASM image library.

claim: Since 2016, Professors Anne Stone and Melissa Wilson contributed tweets featuring genetic and phylogenetic information about combatants citing approximately 175 sources annually.
source: Since 2016, Professors Anne Stone and Melissa Wilson contributed tweets featuring genetic and phylogenetic information about combatants citing an additional ~175 sources annually (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim provides specific information about genetics contributions and is illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: March Mammal Madness was initially created in 2013 as a reaction to a non-science based animal bracket.
source: Although initially created in 2013 as a reaction to a non-science based animal bracket (Cole, 2015) and for psychological resilience in light of other scholarly activities (Clancy et al., 2014; Nelson et al., 2017), March Mammal Madness has grown substantially from its inaugural year.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations.

claim: In response to player and educator feedback and volunteered expertise, the tournament offerings have been refined and expanded each year.
source: In response to player and educator feedback and volunteered expertise, we have refined and expanded the tournament offerings each year (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Biological anthropologists, evolutionary biologists, entomologists, mammalogists, marine biologists, paleoanthropologists, primatologists, and wildlife biologists have been instrumental in crafting battle narratives.
source: Biological anthropologists, evolutionary biologists, entomologists, mammalogists, marine biologists, paleoanthropologists, primatologists, and wildlife biologists have been instrumental, individually and in teams, in crafting battle narratives for the "performance science" of live tweeting the play-by-plays [Anderson, Brokaw, Chestnut, Connors, Dasari, Drew, Durgavich, Hilborn, Hinde, Kissel, Lee, Lewton, Light, Murphy, Tanis, Wilson, Varner] with varying amounts of input from Editors [Anderson, Hinde].
evidence: This claim lists the types of scientists involved and names specific contributors.

claim: The bracket went from janky to elegant in 2016 courtesy of graphic designer Nickley.
source: The bracket went from janky to elegant in 2016 courtesy of graphic designer Nickley, and undergraduate and graduate students have generated sports-style battle summaries that are posted across social media platforms since 2018 [Lesciotto, Krell, Martin].
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated about the bracket design improvement.

claim: Undergraduate and graduate students have generated sports-style battle summaries that are posted across social media platforms since 2018.
source: The bracket went from janky to elegant in 2016 courtesy of graphic designer Nickley, and undergraduate and graduate students have generated sports-style battle summaries that are posted across social media platforms since 2018 [Lesciotto, Krell, Martin].
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated about student contributions.

claim: MC Marmot and the Rodent Roundtable is a sports-style rundown puppet show that was launched independently via YouTube and was an instant hit with school children in 2017.
source: Launched independently via YouTube, MC Marmot and the Rodent Roundtable is a sports-style rundown puppet show that was an instant hit with school children in 2017 [Dietrick, Easterling].
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated about MC Marmot.

claim: In response to an emailed request from the principal of a school serving children with hearing-impairment, MC Marmot added closed-captioning to videos in 2019.
source: In response to an emailed request from the principal of a school in the United States serving children with hearing-impairment, MC Marmot added closed-captioning to videos in 2019.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated about accessibility improvements.

claim: Collaboration is a key component of successful online outreach.
source: Collaboration is a key component of successful online outreach (Bik et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation.

claim: March Mammal Madness serves as an incubator for science communication skill development and media training for trainees and faculty.
source: In addition to the contributions from well-established science communicators, MMM serves as an incubator for SciComm skill development and media training for trainees and faculty.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated about the training benefits of MMM.

claim: Scientists learn to prioritize story-telling and accessible accuracy in science communication, which are more effective with audiences than pedantic attention to inaccessible precision, indecipherable jargon, and overwhelming comprehensiveness.
source: Scientists learn to prioritize story-telling (Neeley et al., 2020) and accessible accuracy in science communication (Yong, 2010), and these techniques are more effective with audiences than the compounding obfuscation generated by pedantic attention to inaccessible precision, indecipherable jargon, and overwhelming comprehensiveness.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations.

claim: Contributors to March Mammal Madness gain visibility, a wider audience through new followers, and an expanded social media network.
source: Contributors to MMM gain visibility, a wider audience through new followers, and an expanded social media network.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated about benefits to contributors.

claim: March Mammal Madness contributors have been featured in media interviews, podcasts, news stories, and blogs that discuss the tournament.
source: Additionally, contributors' study taxa and topics are intentionally showcased in the tournament. MMM contributors have been featured in media interviews, podcasts, news stories, and blogs that discuss the tournament, expanding their media experience and connections with science journalists.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated about media exposure for contributors.

claim: Informal peer-support networks are important in the development of early-career researchers.
source: Moreover, the MMM contributor community supports, mentors, cheers, and cares for each other throughout the year. Informal peer-support networks are important in the development of early-career researchers (Macoun and Miller, 2014), particularly for identities underrepresented in academia (Agosto et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations.

claim: The use of Twitter as a primary platform expands the opportunities for informal mentoring and support and can accommodate the transient aspects of early career stages by facilitating access to colleagues regardless of geographic location.
source: The use of Twitter as a primary platform expands the opportunities for informal mentoring and support and can accommodate the unfortunately transient aspects of early career stages by facilitating access to colleagues and confidants regardless of geographic location (Ferguson and Wheat, 2015).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation.

claim: The most dynamical interactive aspects of March Mammal Madness occur on Twitter.
source: Although tournament content is widely available across multiple social media and website platforms, the most dynamical interactive aspects occur on Twitter.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated about the primary platform for interaction.

claim: Twitter provides the figurative amphitheater allowing spectators to actively engage during the 'battles' and facilitates an active, interconnected community among the citizenry.
source: Twitter not only provides the figurative amphitheater allowing spectators to actively engage during the "battles," but facilitates an active, interconnected community among the citizenry.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated about Twitter's role in community building.

claim: March Mammal Madness reaches many 'publics' and explicitly dismantles boundaries among scientists, students, and the broader members of society.
